title: Space Invaders
description: Space Invaders, released in 1978 by Taito, is the fixed shooter that started the arcade invasion craze. Rows of alien invaders march side to side across the top of the screen, dropping lower with every pass, while the player slides a lone cannon along the bottom and fires upward. Four destructible shields sit between the cannon and the invaders, and the game ends when an invader reaches the ground or the player runs out of cannons.
body:
Space Invaders, released in 1978 by Taito, is the fixed shooter that started the arcade invasion craze. Rows of alien invaders march side to side across the top of the screen, dropping lower with every pass, while the player slides a lone cannon along the bottom and fires upward. Four destructible shields sit between the cannon and the invaders, and the game ends when an invader reaches the ground or the player runs out of cannons.

The tribute demo recreates this idea on a 6-column grid with 2 rows of descending invaders: the player slides a cannon along the bottom, fires upward column by column, and must clear the whole formation before it marches down to row 10. It is an original miniature inspired by the mechanics, not a copy of the arcade game.

The last invader in a column speeds up dramatically, which is why a calm sweep feels safe until the final few aliens start sprinting across the screen. Clearing a column from one side keeps the formation predictable, and saving a shield gap for a retreat lane buys time when the descent quickens.
controls: Type left/right/shoot to move and fire, quit to stop.

title: Space Invaders Part II
description: Space Invaders Part II, Taito's 1979 sequel, keeps the descending formation but adds new tricks: some invaders split into two smaller aliens when hit, and a bonus mothership crosses the top of the screen at intervals. The cabinet art and alien designs grew more elaborate, and the sequel let two players alternate turns, turning a solitary defense into a shared contest.
body:
Space Invaders Part II, Taito's 1979 sequel, keeps the descending formation but adds new tricks: some invaders split into two smaller aliens when hit, and a bonus mothership crosses the top of the screen at intervals. The cabinet art and alien designs grew more elaborate, and the sequel let two players alternate turns, turning a solitary defense into a shared contest.

The tribute demo recreates this idea on a 7-column grid with 3 rows of descending invaders: the player slides a cannon along the bottom, fires upward column by column, and must clear the whole formation before it marches down to row 11. It is an original miniature inspired by the mechanics, not a copy of the arcade game.

Split invaders punish careless shots, because one hit can become two targets instead of none. Players learn to finish a column cleanly rather than peppering the formation, and to watch the top of the screen for the bonus ship without losing track of the lowest row.
controls: Type left/right/shoot to move and fire, quit to stop.

title: Galaxian
description: Galaxian, released by Namco in 1979, took the fixed shooter and gave it color and attitude. Its alien formation sits in neat ranks, but individual aliens break away and dive at the player in swooping paths while firing, so the screen is never a static target range. The bright multi-color sprites and starfield backdrop made it one of the most eye-catching cabinets of its era.
body:
Galaxian, released by Namco in 1979, took the fixed shooter and gave it color and attitude. Its alien formation sits in neat ranks, but individual aliens break away and dive at the player in swooping paths while firing, so the screen is never a static target range. The bright multi-color sprites and starfield backdrop made it one of the most eye-catching cabinets of its era.

The tribute demo recreates this idea on a 8-column grid with 2 rows of descending invaders: the player slides a cannon along the bottom, fires upward column by column, and must clear the whole formation before it marches down to row 12. It is an original miniature inspired by the mechanics, not a copy of the arcade game.

Diving aliens are the danger, not the parked formation, so a good player tracks the diver's curve rather than the rank it left. Holding fire until a diver crosses the cannon's column wastes fewer shots, and the brief pause between dives is the moment to clear stragglers.
controls: Type left/right/shoot to move and fire, quit to stop.

title: Galaga
description: Galaga, Namco's 1981 follow-up to Galaxian, refined the formula into one of the most beloved shooters ever made. Enemies arrive in choreographed swarms, settle into formation, and dive in patterns. Its signature twist is the boss Galaga's tractor beam, which can capture the player's fighter; rescuing it with a spare ship earns a dual fighter that fires twice the shots.
body:
Galaga, Namco's 1981 follow-up to Galaxian, refined the formula into one of the most beloved shooters ever made. Enemies arrive in choreographed swarms, settle into formation, and dive in patterns. Its signature twist is the boss Galaga's tractor beam, which can capture the player's fighter; rescuing it with a spare ship earns a dual fighter that fires twice the shots.

The tribute demo recreates this idea on a 6-column grid with 3 rows of descending invaders: the player slides a cannon along the bottom, fires upward column by column, and must clear the whole formation before it marches down to row 10. It is an original miniature inspired by the mechanics, not a copy of the arcade game.

The dual fighter is worth the risk of a rescue run, but only when a spare ship is available, since a failed rescue costs a life outright. Challenging stages between levels reward pure accuracy, and the best runs treat each enemy entrance pattern as a rehearsed dance.

body:

The player travels through branching warp zones, can upgrade to a triple fighter, and faces larger, more elaborate enemy formations with new attack patterns. It keeps the dive-and-formation heart of the original while adding a sense of travel and choice.

The tribute demo recreates this idea on a 7-column grid with 2 rows of descending invaders: the player slides a cannon along the bottom, fires upward column by column, and must clear the whole formation before it marches down to row 11. Warp choices matter: some routes lead to richer bonus stages and faster upgrades, while others throw denser formations at the player early. The triple fighter widens the firing lane, which changes the safest parking column from the center to a spot that covers two dives at once.

title: Phoenix
description: Phoenix, released in 1980 by Amstar and distributed by Atari and Centuri, is a five-stage fixed shooter with a memorable cast of bird-like enemies. Waves of birds fly in formation, dive, and lay eggs that hatch into new attackers. The final stage brings a huge mothership whose hull must be broken through to reach its pilot, one of the first true boss fights in arcade shooting.

The mothership stage rewards patience: its shield regenerates, so bursts must be timed rather than sprayed. Earlier bird waves teach the rhythm of diving enemies, and a player who survives the egg waves with a shield intact enters the boss fight with room to maneuver.

title: Moon Cresta
description: Moon Cresta, released by Nichibutsu in 1980, builds its shooter around docking. The player starts with a small ship and, after clearing waves, can dock with additional ship sections to gain extra firepower, stacking up to three ships. Losing a docked section costs firepower but not the run, which gives the game a forgiving, layered feel.
body:
Moon Cresta, released by Nichibutsu in 1980, builds its shooter around docking. The player starts with a small ship and, after clearing waves, can dock with additional ship sections to gain extra firepower, stacking up to three ships. Losing a docked section costs firepower but not the run, which gives the game a forgiving, layered feel.

The tribute demo recreates this idea on a 7-column grid with 3 rows of descending invaders: the player slides a cannon along the bottom, fires upward column by column, and must clear the whole formation before it marches down to row 11. It is an original miniature inspired by the mechanics, not a copy of the arcade game.

Docking is the whole strategy: a lone ship is nimble but weak, while a full stack hits hard and presents a bigger target. Experienced players dock early for the firepower, then accept losing a section as the price of surviving a dense wave.

title: Vanguard
description: Vanguard, released by SNK in 1981, mixes fixed shooting with scrolling tunnel stages and a choice of routes. The player's ship can fire in four directions, and the game offers branching paths through zones with different hazards, from asteroid fields to enemy bases. Its energetic soundtrack and varied zones made it a distinctive early shooter.
body:
Vanguard, released by SNK in 1981, mixes fixed shooting with scrolling tunnel stages and a choice of routes. The player's ship can fire in four directions, and the game offers branching paths through zones with different hazards, from asteroid fields to enemy bases. Its energetic soundtrack and varied zones made it a distinctive early shooter.

The tribute demo recreates this idea on a 6-column grid with 2 rows of descending invaders: the player slides a cannon along the bottom, fires upward column by column, and must clear the whole formation before it marches down to row 10. It is an original miniature inspired by the mechanics, not a copy of the arcade game.

Route choice is the strategic core: each zone favors a different firing habit, and the safest path is rarely the most rewarding. Keeping the ship moving diagonally through open space beats hugging a wall, where enemies can pin the player.

title: Stratovox
description: Stratovox, Taito's 1980 shooter, is remembered for its synthesized voice, one of the first in an arcade game, which calls out warnings and taunts as the action unfolds. The player defends astronauts stranded on the right side of the screen, shooting waves of aliens while avoiding hitting the hostages, who can be rescued for bonus points.
body:
Stratovox, Taito's 1980 shooter, is remembered for its synthesized voice, one of the first in an arcade game, which calls out warnings and taunts as the action unfolds. The player defends astronauts stranded on the right side of the screen, shooting waves of aliens while avoiding hitting the hostages, who can be rescued for bonus points.

The tribute demo recreates this idea on a 8-column grid with 2 rows of descending invaders: the player slides a cannon along the bottom, fires upward column by column, and must clear the whole formation before it marches down to row 12. It is an original miniature inspired by the mechanics, not a copy of the arcade game.

The hostage rule changes the shooting calculus: a wild shot that hits a stranded astronaut costs points and pride. The best players fire in short, aimed bursts and let an alien pass rather than risk a rescue target.

title: Ozma Wars
description: Ozma Wars, SNK's 1979 fixed shooter, is one of the earliest games of its kind, predating the flood of invasion-style cabinets. The player defends against waves of alien ships with an energy bar that drains as the ship takes hits and refills between stages, an early attempt at a health system rather than one-hit deaths.
body:
Ozma Wars, SNK's 1979 fixed shooter, is one of the earliest games of its kind, predating the flood of invasion-style cabinets. The player defends against waves of alien ships with an energy bar that drains as the ship takes hits and refills between stages, an early attempt at a health system rather than one-hit deaths.

The tribute demo recreates this idea on a 6-column grid with 3 rows of descending invaders: the player slides a cannon along the bottom, fires upward column by column, and must clear the whole formation before it marches down to row 10. It is an original miniature inspired by the mechanics, not a copy of the arcade game.

The energy bar forgives a single mistake but not a habit of them, so the long game is about avoiding damage entirely rather than trading hits. Players who learn the earliest, simplest waves find the later energy economy much easier to manage.
controls: Type left/right/shoot to move and fire, quit to stop.
